item.title: Clai Command Line AI: Stdin to LLM to Stdout — A Unix-Philosophy Review
item.description: Clai is a minimalist Go CLI tool that pipes stdin through an LLM to stdout — no sessions, no REPL, no lock-in. Here is how it compares to llm, fabric, aichat, and mods.
item.content:encoded:
What Is Clai? — Stdin to LLM to Stdout

Clai is a command-line AI tool that reads text from standard input, sends it to a large language model, and writes the response to standard output. That is it. No interactive REPL, no session state, no chat history, no plugin ecosystem, no GUI. Written in Go and released as a single binary, Clai embodies the Unix philosophy: do one thing well and compose with other tools via pipes. At version 0.3.0 as of July 2026, it is an early-stage project with a clear philosophical stance that sets it apart from every other AI CLI tool on the market.

Why Does the Unix Philosophy Matter for AI Tools?

Doug McIlroy, the inventor of Unix pipes, famously said: “Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface.” Clai is the first AI CLI tool to take this principle literally. Every other tool in the space has drifted toward platforms — adding sessions, plugins, chat modes, RAG pipelines, and agent frameworks. Clai refuses all of that by design.

The practical consequence is composability. Because Clai reads stdin and writes stdout, it fits into any existing shell pipeline:

git diff --cached | clai "Write a concise commit message" | pbcopy
curl https://example.com/article | clai "Summarize in 3 bullet points"
cat server.log | grep ERROR | clai "Explain what went wrong"

No other AI CLI tool integrates this cleanly because none of them are pure stdin/stdout tools. They all introduce some form of state, formatting, or interactive mode that breaks the pipe contract.

The Anti-Platform Bet

The AI industry is racing to build platforms that capture users inside ecosystems. Clai makes the opposite bet: the terminal is already the platform. By refusing to add session state, Clai ensures that no user workflow becomes dependent on Clai itself. You can replace Clai with any other stdin/stdout tool tomorrow without changing your pipelines. This is a radical idea in 2026, when most AI tools are designed to maximize switching costs.

What Are the Key Features of Clai?

Despite its minimalist philosophy, Clai packs meaningful functionality into its small surface area.

Built-in Prompt System

Clai ships with a collection of curated prompts stored as Markdown files. Users can invoke them by name:

cat code.py | clai --prompt explain-code
cat README.md | clai --prompt improve-writing

Prompts are plain Markdown files with a simple frontmatter format. The community can contribute prompts without a package manager — just open a pull request. This is the Unix way: prompts are text files, not plugins.

Multi-Provider Support

Clai supports six LLM providers out of the box:

Provider Type Notes
OpenAI Cloud GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini
Anthropic Cloud Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus
Google Gemini Cloud Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 1.5 Flash
Vertex AI Cloud Enterprise GCP deployment
AWS Bedrock Cloud Enterprise AWS deployment
Ollama Local Fully offline, no data leaves your machine

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint also works, which covers hundreds of self-hosted and proxy options. This provider flexibility means Clai can be the single interface to every LLM you use, whether local or cloud.

Reasoning Strategies

Clai supports four reasoning strategies that control how the LLM processes input:

  1. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) — The model reasons step by step before answering. Best for math, logic, and multi-step problems.
  2. Tree-of-Thought (ToT) — The model explores multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. Better for open-ended creative tasks.
  3. Chain-of-Draft (CoD) — The model produces concise intermediate reasoning. Faster and cheaper than full CoT.
  4. Self-Refine — The model generates an answer, critiques it, and refines it. Best for writing and code review.

These strategies are applied via prompt engineering at the CLI level, not through model-specific APIs, which means they work across all supported providers.

Structured Output

Clai can return structured data (JSON, YAML, CSV) by specifying an output format flag. This makes it usable in automated pipelines where the output feeds into another program:

cat changelog.md | clai --format json "Extract version numbers and dates"

The structured output mode is critical for Clai’s pipeline-native design — it turns the LLM into a data transformation tool, not just a text generator.

How Does Clai Compare to Alternatives?

The AI CLI tool landscape has several established players. Here is how Clai stacks up against the four main competitors.

Feature Comparison Table

Feature Clai llm (simonw) fabric aichat mods (Charm)
Language Go Python Go Rust Go
GitHub Stars ~3 12,316 43,329 10,329 4,531
Stdin/Stdout Only Yes No No No No
Session/Chat Mode No Yes No Yes Yes
Plugin System No Yes Yes (patterns) Yes No
Local LLM Support Yes (Ollama) Yes Yes Yes Yes
Reasoning Strategies 4 (CoT, ToT, CoD, Self-Refine) No No No No
Structured Output Yes Yes Partial Yes No
Pre-built Binaries Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes
License MIT Apache 2.0 MIT MIT MIT
Release Stage v0.3.0 (early) v1.x (mature) v1.x (mature) v1.x (mature) Deprecated

When to Choose Each Tool

Choose Clai if you want a pure pipeline tool that composes with grep, jq, curl, and git. You value the Unix philosophy and want zero lock-in. You are comfortable with an early-stage project (v0.3.0) and willing to watch it grow.

Choose llm (simonw/llm) if you want a mature Python tool with a rich plugin ecosystem. Simon Willison’s llm has 12,316 GitHub stars, supports dozens of models through plugins, and has session/chat mode. It is the most popular general-purpose CLI LLM tool for good reason.

Choose fabric (danielmiessler/fabric) if you want a curated ecosystem of AI patterns and prompts. With 43,329 GitHub stars, fabric is the most starred AI CLI framework. Its pattern system is more opinionated and comprehensive than Clai’s prompt collection, but it is also a heavier dependency.

Choose aichat (sigoden/aichat) if you want an all-in-one tool with RAG, function calling, and agent capabilities. Aichat supports 10+ LLM providers and has the richest feature set. It is the opposite of Clai’s minimalism — which is exactly what some users want.

Do not choose mods (charmbracelet/mods) — it has been deprecated in favor of other Charm tools. Its 4,531 stars reflect past popularity, but the project is no longer maintained.

The Minimalism Spectrum

Pure pipe tool ← Clai · llm · fabric · aichat → Full platform

Clai sits at the far left of this spectrum. Every other tool has drifted rightward by adding features that break the pipe contract. This is not inherently good or bad — it is a design trade-off. But it means Clai occupies a niche that no other actively maintained tool fills.

How Do You Get Started with Clai?

Installation is straightforward. Clai provides pre-built binaries for macOS (both Intel and Apple Silicon) and Linux (both amd64 and arm64). You can also install via Homebrew tap or go install.

Quick Install

# Homebrew
brew install maxrodrigo/tap/clai

# Go install
go install github.com/maxrodrigo/clai@latest

# Or download a binary from GitHub Releases

Basic Configuration

Clai needs at least one LLM provider configured. The simplest path is Ollama for fully local operation:

# Set up Ollama provider
clai config set provider ollama
clai config set model llama3.1

# Or use OpenAI
clai config set provider openai
clai config set model gpt-4o-mini
clai config set openai-api-key sk-...

Your First Pipeline

Once configured, Clai works in any shell pipeline:

# Summarize a web page
curl -s https://example.com/long-article | clai "Summarize this in 3 sentences"

# Explain an error
echo "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')" | clai "Explain this error and suggest a fix"

# Translate text
echo "Bonjour le monde" | clai --prompt translate-to-english

# Extract structured data
ps aux | clai --format json "List the top 5 memory-consuming processes"

Each command reads from stdin, processes through the LLM, and writes to stdout. You can pipe the output into anything: pbcopy, > file.md, | grep, | jq, or another clai invocation.

Who Is Clai For?

Clai is not for everyone. Its design makes deliberate trade-offs that serve specific users well.

Ideal Clai Users

Unix enthusiasts who believe in the pipe philosophy and want AI tools that respect it. If you reach for grep, awk, and jq before opening a GUI, Clai will feel natural.

Pipeline builders who need AI as a composable step in automated workflows. CI/CD scripts, data processing pipelines, and code review automation benefit from a tool that never blocks on interactive input.

Privacy-conscious developers who run local models via Ollama. Clai’s provider-agnostic design means you can use it entirely offline with no data leaving your machine.

Terminal power users who want a single AI interface across multiple providers. Clai’s provider abstraction lets you switch between OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and local models with a config change — no tool switching.

Who Should Look Elsewhere

Chat-oriented users who want an interactive AI conversation in the terminal. Clai has no session mode. Use aichat or llm with its chat subcommand instead.

Plugin seekers who want to extend the tool with custom functionality. Clai has no plugin system. Prompts are the only extension point.

Enterprise teams who need a mature, battle-tested tool with a large community. Clai is v0.3.0 with approximately 3 GitHub stars. It is a promising project, not a production-grade platform.

Verdict: Early but Promising

Clai is the most philosophically consistent AI CLI tool available in 2026. It is the only tool that fully commits to the Unix pipe model — stdin to LLM to stdout, nothing else. This purity is both its greatest strength and its most significant limitation.

Strengths

  • True pipe composability — works with any Unix tool in any pipeline
  • Zero lock-in — no session state, no proprietary format, no switching costs
  • Multi-provider — one interface for local and cloud LLMs
  • Reasoning strategies — unique feature not found in any competitor
  • Structured output — JSON, YAML, CSV for automated consumption
  • Single binary — written in Go, no runtime dependencies

Limitations

  • Very early stage — v0.3.0 with minimal community adoption
  • No session/chat — intentional, but limits use cases
  • No plugin system — prompts only, no code extensions
  • Small community — approximately 3 GitHub stars at launch
  • Limited documentation — early-stage project documentation

The Bottom Line

Clai is worth your attention if you value the Unix philosophy and want an AI tool that amplifies your existing workflow instead of replacing it. It is not ready to replace llm or fabric for most users today, but its design direction is the right one for a specific and underserved niche. Watch this project — if it gains community traction, it could become the jq of AI tools: small, focused, and indispensable.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Clai free to use?

Yes, Clai is open source under the MIT License. The tool itself costs nothing. You pay only for the LLM API calls you make through your chosen provider, or nothing at all if you use a local model via Ollama.

Does Clai work with local LLMs?

Yes. Clai supports Ollama out of the box, which lets you run models like Llama 3.1, Mistral, and Gemma entirely on your own machine. No data ever leaves your computer when using local models.

How is Clai different from simonw/llm?

Clai is a pure stdin/stdout pipeline tool with no session state, no chat mode, and no plugin system. Simon Willison’s llm has sessions, plugins, and a chat REPL. Clai is minimalist by design; llm is a platform. They serve different philosophies and different use cases.

Can I use Clai in CI/CD pipelines?

Yes. Because Clai reads stdin and writes stdout with no interactive mode, it is ideal for automated pipelines. The structured output flag (–format json) makes it easy to parse results programmatically in scripts.

What reasoning strategies does Clai support?

Clai supports four reasoning strategies: Chain-of-Thought (step-by-step reasoning), Tree-of-Thought (multiple parallel reasoning paths), Chain-of-Draft (concise intermediate reasoning), and Self-Refine (generate, critique, refine). These are applied via prompt engineering and work across all supported LLM providers.

item.title: JetBrains Go AI Coding Agent 2026: Junie Review, Free Tier, and Smarter Assistance
item.description: JetBrains unified AI strategy with Junie coding agent and AI Assistant. Free tier, pricing, SWE-Rebench 61.6% solve rate, and GoLand-specific AI features reviewed.
item.content:encoded:
JetBrains has unified its AI offerings under a single subscription model that includes both the AI Assistant and the Junie coding agent, with a free tier that provides unlimited code completion and local AI models at no cost. This review examines how JetBrains’ Go AI coding agent ecosystem — spanning Junie, AI Assistant, and GoLand-specific features — performs in 2026, covering pricing, benchmark results, real-world user feedback, and how it compares to alternatives like GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Windsurf.

What Is JetBrains’ Unified AI Strategy in 2026?

JetBrains has consolidated all its AI capabilities — AI Assistant and Junie — under a single subscription framework. Instead of maintaining separate products with disjointed pricing, the company now offers three tiers: AI Free, AI Pro, and AI Ultimate. The key differentiator is that every tier includes access to both the AI Assistant (chat-based code help) and Junie (the autonomous coding agent), with quotas scaling by tier.

This unified approach stands in contrast to the fragmented AI tooling landscape where developers often juggle separate subscriptions for GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and standalone chat tools. With over 11.4 million developers using JetBrains AI infrastructure on Google Cloud as of April 2025, the platform has significant scale and momentum.

What Does the JetBrains AI Free Tier Include?

The AI Free tier is surprisingly generous. It includes:

  • Unlimited code completion — full-line and multi-line completions with no credit cap
  • Local AI models — run models on your own hardware for completions and chat
  • Cloud AI credits — a limited monthly quota for cloud-powered AI Assistant queries and Junie agentic tasks

This free tier effectively removes the cost barrier for JetBrains users to adopt AI-assisted development. For Go developers using the free tier of GoLand (or evaluating it), this means immediate access to AI code completion without any payment. The local model support is particularly valuable for developers concerned about data privacy or working in air-gapped environments.

What Is Junie and How Does It Work?

Junie is JetBrains’ native AI coding agent that operates directly inside JetBrains IDEs and, as of 2026, as a standalone CLI tool. Unlike cloud-only agents that work with a text-based representation of your code, Junie leverages the full power of the IntelliJ platform — its inspection engine, refactoring APIs, test runner, and build system integration.

How Does Junie’s IDE-Native Architecture Give It an Edge?

Junie doesn’t just see your code as text. It understands your project’s structure through the IDE’s own analysis engine. This means it can:

  • Detect build errors and compilation failures in real time
  • Run tests and interpret test output to fix broken code
  • Read Git history to understand what changed and why
  • Execute terminal commands autonomously within the IDE
  • Make multi-file edits that respect your project’s existing architecture

The agent operates in three modes:

Mode Description Best For
Code mode Full autonomous agent — proposes plans, writes code across files, runs tests, iterates on failures Complex multi-step tasks, feature implementation
Chat mode Conversational AI Assistant with context-aware answers Quick questions, code explanations, debugging help
CLI mode Terminal-based Junie (shipped 2026) with BYOK and OpenRouter support CI/CD pipelines, non-JetBrains editors, automation

Junie uses a “plan on a powerful model, implement on a fast one” routing strategy. Complex planning is delegated to a frontier model (like Claude 3.7 Sonnet or Gemini 2.5 Pro), while implementation runs on a faster, more cost-efficient model. This architectural choice is a major reason for Junie’s cost efficiency.

Which IDEs Support Junie?

Junie is compatible with eight JetBrains IDEs:

  • IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate
  • PyCharm Pro
  • WebStorm
  • GoLand
  • PhpStorm
  • Rider
  • RustRover
  • RubyMine

The 2026 CLI release extends Junie to any terminal environment, including CI/CD pipelines, and supports bring-your-own-key (BYOK) and OpenRouter for model access. This means developers using VS Code, Neovim, or other editors can still leverage Junie through the command line.

How Does Junie Perform on Benchmarks?

Junie achieves a 61.6% solve rate on SWE-Rebench at a cost of $1.14 per problem. This is approximately 4x cheaper than the next-best competitor, which costs $4.91 per solved task. At launch in January 2025, Junie scored 53.6% on SWE-bench Verified, and the current 61.6% on SWE-Rebench (72.7% pass@5) represents meaningful improvement over 18 months of development.

Metric Junie Competitor Average
SWE-Rebench solve rate 61.6% ~45-55%
Cost per solved problem $1.14 $4.91
SWE-bench Verified (launch) 53.6% —
Pass@5 (SWE-Rebench) 72.7% —

How Has the AI Assistant Become Smarter?

The AI Assistant in JetBrains IDEs has evolved significantly. It now supports multiple frontier models including Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, the latest OpenAI models, and local models running on your own hardware.

What Is the New Agent Mode and Multi-File Editing?

The most significant upgrade to AI Assistant is the new edit mode that enables seamless multi-file edits directly from the chat interface. Instead of suggesting changes one file at a time, the AI Assistant can now propose and apply modifications across multiple files in a single operation. This bridges the gap between simple chat-based assistance and full agentic behavior.

The AI Assistant also benefits from the same deep IDE integration as Junie — it understands your project’s type system, build configuration, and dependency graph, making its suggestions more contextually accurate than generic AI chat tools.

What AI Features Are Specific to GoLand?

For Go developers, GoLand’s AI integration offers several specialized capabilities:

  • Struct generation — AI can generate Go struct definitions from natural language descriptions or JSON schemas
  • Interface implementation — automatically implement Go interfaces with proper method signatures
  • Test generation — create table-driven tests with realistic test cases
  • Error handling patterns — AI suggests idiomatic Go error handling based on project conventions
  • Concurrency assistance — help with goroutine patterns, channel usage, and sync primitives

These Go-specific features leverage the AI Assistant’s understanding of Go idioms and best practices, making suggestions that align with the language’s conventions rather than generic patterns.

JetBrains AI Pricing: Free vs Pro vs Ultimate

Tier Price Code Completion AI Assistant Junie Credits Local Models
Free $0 Unlimited Limited cloud credits Limited cloud credits Yes
Pro $100/user/year ($8/month) Unlimited Increased quotas Increased quotas Yes
Ultimate $300/user/year ($20-40/month) Unlimited Maximum quotas Maximum quotas Yes

The All Products Pack and dotUltimate subscriptions include AI Pro at no additional cost, making them attractive for developers who use multiple JetBrains IDEs.

The credit-based consumption model means that heavy users of Junie’s agentic features may find the Ultimate tier more cost-effective, while developers who primarily use code completion and occasional chat queries may never need to upgrade from the Free tier.

How Does JetBrains AI Compare to GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Windsurf?

Feature JetBrains AI (Junie + Assistant) GitHub Copilot Cursor Windsurf
IDE-native Yes (deep IntelliJ integration) Partial (VS Code native, limited elsewhere) VS Code fork VS Code fork
Free tier Yes (unlimited completion + local models) Limited (2K completions/month) Limited Limited
Autonomous agent Junie (Code mode + CLI) Copilot Agent (preview) Agent mode Cascade
Multi-IDE support 8 IDEs + CLI VS Code, JetBrains (limited) VS Code only VS Code only
Model choice Claude, Gemini, GPT, local, OpenRouter GPT-4o only GPT-4o, Claude GPT-4o, Claude
CLI support Yes (Junie CLI 2026) No No No
SWE-Rebench 61.6% ~33% ~45% ~40%
Cost per task $1.14 ~$5+ ~$3-5 ~$3-5

JetBrains’ key advantages are its deep IDE integration (not a VS Code fork), broad multi-IDE support, model choice flexibility, and cost efficiency. The main limitation is that full Junie agentic capabilities require a paid tier and are only available on premium IDE editions.

What Do Real Users Say About Junie?

Hacker News discussion (174 points, 126 comments) reveals strong sentiment:

Positive feedback:

  • “Junie completely replaced Claude Code and Cursor payments” — several users reported canceling other AI tool subscriptions after adopting Junie
  • “Least aggressive agent, no complete rewrites, achieves ~95% of what I ask” — users appreciate Junie’s conservative approach to code changes
  • Deep IDE integration means Junie understands build errors and test failures natively

Concerns:

  • Memory usage — Junie can be resource-intensive, especially on larger projects
  • Pricing model — credit-based consumption can be unpredictable for heavy users
  • Premium IDE requirement — Junie only works with paid IDE editions (Ultimate/Pro)
  • MCP support works but can be slow due to server load

A notable feature is the .noai file — placing this at a project root disables all AI support, giving teams fine-grained control over which projects use AI assistance.

What Are the Pros and Cons of JetBrains AI for Go Development?

Pros:

  • Deep IDE integration that understands Go project structure, build system, and test framework
  • Free tier with unlimited code completion and local models — no cost to try
  • Cost efficiency — $1.14 per solved task is 4x cheaper than competitors
  • Model choice — use Claude, Gemini, GPT, or local models
  • Multi-platform — works across all JetBrains IDEs and CLI
  • Go-specific features — struct generation, interface implementation, test generation
  • Conservative agent behavior — less likely to make destructive changes

Cons:

  • Full agentic features require paid IDE editions (Ultimate/Pro)
  • Credit-based consumption can be unpredictable
  • Memory usage can be high on large projects
  • Not available for VS Code or other editors natively (CLI is the bridge)
  • MCP integration still maturing

Conclusion: Is JetBrains AI the Right Choice for Go Developers in 2026?

For Go developers already using JetBrains GoLand, the AI Free tier alone provides immediate value with unlimited code completion and local model support. The upgrade to AI Pro ($100/year) unlocks meaningful Junie agentic capabilities that can handle multi-step coding tasks, test generation, and refactoring at a cost that is significantly cheaper than alternatives.

The combination of deep IDE integration, model choice, and the new CLI mode makes JetBrains AI a compelling option even for developers who don’t use JetBrains IDEs as their primary editor. The 61.6% SWE-Rebench solve rate and 4x cost advantage over competitors suggest that JetBrains has built not just a competitive AI coding agent, but arguably the most cost-effective one available in 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is JetBrains AI free to use?

Yes, JetBrains offers an AI Free tier that includes unlimited code completion, local AI models, and limited cloud credits for AI Assistant and Junie. No payment is required to get started.

Does Junie work with GoLand?

Yes, Junie is fully compatible with GoLand. It supports Go-specific features including struct generation, interface implementation, test generation, and concurrency assistance.

How much does JetBrains AI Pro cost?

AI Pro costs $100 per user per year or $8 per month. It includes increased quotas for cloud AI and Junie agentic tasks. The All Products Pack and dotUltimate subscriptions include AI Pro at no extra cost.

How does Junie compare to GitHub Copilot?

Junie achieves a 61.6% solve rate on SWE-Rebench compared to Copilot’s ~33%, costs $1.14 per solved task versus ~$5+, and offers model choice (Claude, Gemini, GPT, local) versus Copilot’s GPT-4o only. Junie also provides a standalone CLI and works across 8 JetBrains IDEs.

Can I use Junie without a JetBrains IDE?

Yes, Junie CLI was shipped in 2026 and works in any terminal or CI/CD pipeline. It supports bring-your-own-key (BYOK) and OpenRouter for model access, making it usable from VS Code, Neovim, or any editor.
